lesson.title: f, f-Prime, f-Double-Prime: The Family Resemblance
lesson.summary: The graphs of a function and its first and second derivatives are locked in a strict correspondence, where every rise, fall, peak, valley, and bend in one graph encodes an exact feature of the other two.
lesson.body:
Curve sketching treats f, f', and f'' as three separate tools applied to one function. It is worth stopping to look at them side by side, because the relationships between them are not loose analogies; they are exact, testable correspondences. Wherever f is increasing, f' is positive. Wherever f is decreasing, f' is negative. Wherever f has a local extremum, f' is zero and changes sign, which is exactly the First Derivative Test. Wherever f is concave up, f'' is positive, which is the same thing as saying f' is increasing there. Wherever f is concave down, f'' is negative, meaning f' is decreasing. And wherever f has an inflection point, f'' is zero and changes sign, which means f' has a local extremum of its own at that point, by the same First Derivative Test logic, just one derivative up the chain.

That last correspondence, an inflection point of f lining up with a local extremum of f', is the one students most often miss, so it is worth watching happen in a single example. Let f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2. Then f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2), with roots at x = 0 and x = 2, and f''(x) = 6x - 6, which is zero at x = 1.

Checking the sign of f': for x < 0, both x and (x - 2) are negative, so their product is positive, giving f' > 0; for 0 < x < 2, x is positive and (x - 2) is negative, giving f' < 0; for x > 2, both factors are positive, giving f' > 0 again. So f increases, then decreases, then increases, with a local maximum at x = 0 (f(0) = 0) and a local minimum at x = 2 (f(2) = 8 - 12 = -4).

Now check f'' at those same two points as a consistency test. The Second Derivative Test says a local max should have f'' < 0 and a local min should have f'' > 0. Here f''(0) = 6(0) - 6 = -6, negative, matching the local maximum; and f''(2) = 6(2) - 6 = 6, positive, matching the local minimum. Both checks pass.

The more interesting point is x = 1, the zero of f''. Since f''(x) = 6x - 6 is negative for x < 1 and positive for x > 1, f is concave down before x = 1 and concave up after, so x = 1 is a genuine inflection point, with f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2. But look at what this means for f': f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x is itself an upward-opening parabola, and f''(x) = 6x - 6 being its derivative means f' has a critical point exactly at x = 1, where f'' = 0. Since f'' goes from negative to positive there, f' is decreasing then increasing, so x = 1 is a local minimum of f', with f'(1) = 3 - 6 = -3. In graph terms, the inflection point of f is exactly where the curve is falling most steeply, the single most negative slope on the whole descending stretch between the local max and the local min. That is the family resemblance in action: a feature that looks like a subtle bend in the graph of f (an inflection point) is the same feature that looks like an obvious low point (a local minimum) one derivative down in the graph of f'.
